# Introduction {.unnumbered}

*From Concept to Silicon* is a general reference for designing open systems-on-chip: specifying reusable hardware, implementing SystemVerilog RTL, checking its behavior, integrating processors and peripherals, and evaluating FPGA and ASIC implementations. It is written for university students, instructors and engineers learning or extending an open hardware workflow.

CORE-V Wally provides a concrete RISC-V processor and SoC hierarchy. Small components make design decisions tractable before they appear inside a larger platform. A signed dot-product accelerator connects specification, independent models, interfaces, firmware, verification and implementation evidence across the book. The objective is to explain the engineering decisions between these stages and make their assumptions inspectable.

The book can be read as a reference or followed through one of three routes. It does not require enrolment in a particular degree; an optional twelve-week course built on it is documented separately in @sec-hsd-coursework.

## Choose your route {#sec-choose-route}

| Route | Choose it if you want to… | Start with | You finish with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **[Foundations](#sec-foundations-route)** | learn or refresh RTL, verification and basic synthesis on small blocks | [The RISC-V ISA](chapters/01-foundations/risc-v-isa.qmd) | A parameterized block with independent tests, an explained failure and repair, a scoped formal result and a generic synthesis report |
| **[Complete SoC](#sec-complete-soc-route)** | integrate a processor, peripherals and firmware, then take the design to an FPGA | [CORE-V Wally](chapters/02-risc-v-cores/core-v-wally.qmd), after the Foundations chapters | A software-controlled system with firmware and interrupt evidence, plus an FPGA implementation dossier at a stated boundary |
| **[ASIC Design](#sec-asic-design-route)** | follow a verified block through placement, routing and physical checks | [VLSI design](chapters/06-asic-implementation/vlsi-design.qmd), with a verified RTL block in hand | A block taken to GDSII, with its configuration, reports and an acceptance decision |

: Routes through the book and where to start {#tbl-intro-routes-through-book-where tbl-colwidths="[21,26,19,34]"}

No route needs a physical FPGA; the [route without a board](labs/NO-FPGA.md) keeps the simulation and report-analysis work. Each route is described below, and the [route map](learning-paths.qmd#sec-route-map) gives a step-by-step sequence for each.

## Prerequisites and working approach

Start with combinational/sequential logic, finite-state machines, basic processor organization, C and simple assembly. Being able to edit files and interpret a compiler or simulator error is useful. The Foundations Route reinforces RTL semantics, state, widths, reset and timing before larger integration work depends on them.

SystemVerilog remains the principal RTL language. The generator example introduces Chisel and CIRCT as an optional comparison. Shell commands, Git, Python and containers support reproducibility; a container image supplies tools rather than replacing the design contract. The [reproduction appendix](appendices/reproducible-labs.qmd) distinguishes checked recipes, adaptation templates and student design exercises.

A hardware result is only as useful as the story behind it. At each stage, keep four things together: the requirement, the implementation and configuration, an independent check, and the observed result. That is what lets a colleague rerun your work and see the same thing. An unchanged reference run gives you a baseline to compare against; when you change the design, collect new evidence, including the failures, because that is where most of the learning happens. The common methodology in @sec-verification-methodology applies from a small RTL unit to platform and physical implementation.

## A Foundations Route {#sec-foundations-route}

Follow the ISA, SystemVerilog, microarchitecture and clocking chapters, then the verification methodology and one simulation frontend. Use a small arithmetic block, register file or ready/valid buffer to connect a specification to state transitions and edge-level checks. Choose Verilator/C++ or cocotb/Python before adding a second frontend for comparison.

The dedicated [formal-verification chapter](chapters/03-simulation-verification/formal-verification.qmd) develops an executable FIFO through assertions, assumptions, useful-traffic witnesses, BMC, induction, counterexamples, repair and equivalence. It supplies a manageable next step after a self-checking simulation. Full-processor proofs remain advanced work.

**Destination:** a small parameterized RTL component with independent tests, an explained failure and repair, a scoped formal result, and a generic synthesis report. Most small-block activities use the ordinary laboratory container without a board. Consult the [route map](learning-paths.qmd#sec-route-map) for concrete starting points and compute labels.

## A Complete SoC Route {#sec-complete-soc-route}

Build on the Foundations Route with Wally hierarchy/configuration, memory and transport contracts, buses, interrupts, peripherals and firmware. Follow the executable AXI/DMA project in @sec-executable-project: specify the arithmetic and register interface, test the IP independently, then connect the CPU adapter, shared memory, driver and interrupt completion.

The FPGA chapters introduce synthesis, clock/interface constraints, mapping, placement/routing and board bring-up. The Nexys Video route includes clocking and LiteDRAM integration. Distinguish an IP implementation, a board boundary fixture and the complete processor platform when interpreting counts and timing. Booting Linux and adding its driver are useful continuations after the bare-metal integration works.

**Destination:** an integrated processor/peripheral system with repeatable firmware and interrupt evidence, plus an FPGA implementation/report dossier at a stated boundary. A connected board adds physical observations. The [route without a board](labs/NO-FPGA.md) preserves simulation and implementation-report analysis. Full-Wally RTL builds, DDR bring-up and Linux tool/model builds require more resources than a unit test; the activity labels identify that change in scale.

## An ASIC Design Route {#sec-asic-design-route}

Start from a verified RTL block and the synthesis/constraint material. Study the VLSI/PPA foundations, RTL-to-GDSII stages, OpenROAD, LibreLane and physical validation/DFT. Follow a mapped netlist into floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and extracted timing. Use the measured studies to connect a failing path or electrical limit to a change in RTL, constraints or physical optimization.

@sec-complete-case carries the same accelerator into an ASIC block and compares it with FPGA implementations. @sec-complete-closure continues from timing violations to an accepted block within a declared single-corner gate. @sec-layout-verification adds actual reference-PDK DRC/LVS and power/body finishing, while retaining the distinction between a public reference technology and foundry manufacturing qualification.

**Destination:** a reproducible block implementation through GDSII, its configuration/technology manifest, physical views and reports, and a precise acceptance decision. Reading supplied results can precede running the larger tools. Producing GDSII is not by itself a complete manufacturing release, and this book does not physically implement the complete Wally SoC.

## Depth and activity labels

These three technical routes describe **what** to study. The **Core Learning Path** and **Advanced Reference Path** describe how to select depth and workload within them. They share one complete edition, one set of source examples and stable chapter links. The Core Learning Path is the bounded twelve-week course adoption described in @sec-hsd-coursework.

The Advanced Reference Path includes optional deeper studies of RVV, multicore, PMU design, out-of-order processors, Linux integration, security mechanisms, architectural exploration and extended physical closure. Advanced describes curricular scope, not a universal compute cost: a small security or memory-ordering model may run cheaply, while a full FPGA implementation can demand substantial resources.

Each labelled activity states its role and compute class. A `C0 review / C3 rerun` label distinguishes interpreting supplied physical reports from executing the implementation campaign. A separate board indicator identifies physical observations. The [label legend](learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels) and downloadable activity catalogue support instructors adapting the book to another course and independent readers choosing a practical sequence.

## One component across the routes

The common dot-product project makes the transitions comparable. Its manifest connects numerical behavior, RTL, independent tests, bounded formal checks, real-Wally firmware/interrupts, FPGA placement/routing and ASIC block implementation. The source lock and evidence records let a reader ask which stage changed and which results remain applicable.

The case study is explicit about scale, and that is what makes its numbers useful. The complete Wally system runs in RTL simulation, while the FPGA and ASIC results describe the accelerator IP or a named fixture. Functional evidence, generic synthesis, routed timing, power estimates and manufacturing checks each answer a different question; knowing which one you are holding tells you what to do next when you replace an algorithm, memory interface, platform or technology.

The reusable-IP continuation packages supported configurations, generated register views, dependencies, models and constraints for another integrator. The CI experiment then checks contracts, independent tests, bounded properties and a reviewed logical-cost budget on each candidate. These practices are useful whether the reader follows a taught course, a professional project or an independent study plan.

## Key ideas {#review-intro-ideas .unnumbered .unlisted}

- The book is a general SoC reference with three technical entry routes.
- The twelve-week course is one adoption, with its own outcomes and assessment.
- Experiment role, compute cost and physical evidence are separate decisions.

## What you should now be able to explain {#review-intro-explain .unnumbered .unlisted}

Choose a technical route, identify its next deliverable and distinguish a local block check from a platform build or a physical qualification claim.

## Common mistakes {#review-intro-mistakes .unnumbered .unlisted}

It is tempting to treat every experiment as required coursework, but the book is a reference to select from. Advanced topics are not always expensive, so check the compute label before ruling one out. And a reference result belongs to the RTL that produced it: once you modify the design, collect new evidence.

## Try it yourself {#review-intro-try .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Preparation · C0](learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-intro-review .learning-activity}

Choose a route and one component. Write its next requirement, expected evidence, compute class and any dependency you need before executing the experiment.
